title: Creatives and claims
summary: What you can and cannot say in forex, CFD and crypto ads, where risk warnings must sit to be seen, and how to build honest angles, visuals and UGC that still convert. You finish with a creative pipeline, a compliance log and a rule card for killing, scaling and refreshing trading creatives.

lessons.title: The claims map: what you can and cannot say
objectives: By the end you can sort any trading ad claim into red, amber or green.
By the end you can spot implied claims hidden in images, props and layouts.
By the end you can run a claim audit on a draft ad and keep proof on file.

steps.h: Why every word in a trading ad matters
steps.p: In many countries an ad for a broker or exchange is a financial promotion, so the law treats it like the broker's own advertising. One false claim can get the ad rejected, the ad account restricted, your payouts withheld and, in some places, break the law. The words you choose carry real money and real risk.
steps.more: Example: you run three ad sets at $50 a day. One ad says 'make $200 a day from your phone'. The platform restricts the ad account for policy breaches. Spend stops, the $1,800 of qualified FTDs still in the network's hold period is reviewed, and the network's terms let it withhold payouts for non-compliant traffic. The cost of that one sentence is far more than the ad ever earned. Figures are illustrative, not a statistic about any network.

steps.h: Six kinds of claim in trading ads
steps.p: Almost every sentence in a trading ad falls into one of six kinds. Naming the kind first tells you how risky it is before you even read the details. Outcome, ease and safety claims are where most trouble starts.
d: Outcome|'earn', 'profit', 'income', 'double your money'
Performance|win rates, past returns, 'my results'
Ease|'anyone can', 'no experience needed', 'autopilot'
Safety|'no risk', 'protected', 'guaranteed'
Product fact|spreads, fees, minimum deposit, demo account
Education|what leverage is, how a stop-loss works
steps.say: Almost every sentence in a trading ad is one of six kinds of claim. Look at the cards. Outcome: earn, profit, income, double your money. Performance: win rates, past returns, my results. Ease: anyone can, no experience needed, autopilot. Safety: no risk, protected, guaranteed. Product fact: spreads, fees, minimum deposit, demo account. And education: what leverage is, how a stop-loss works. Naming the kind first tells you how risky it is. Outcome, ease and safety claims are where most trouble starts.

steps.p: Use this as a starting list, not legal advice. Red claims never run. Amber claims run only if true, sourced and approved in writing by the broker for that geo. Green claims are still checked, but they are where honest ads live.

steps.say: Here's the red, amber and green list. It's a starting list, not legal advice. Red claims never run: earn three hundred dollars a week trading, a ninety two percent win rate, risk-free trading. Amber claims run only if true, sourced and approved in writing by the broker for that geo: spreads from point six pips, true only for some accounts and pairs, or licensed by a named regulator, which must match the entity users sign with. Green claims, like practise on a free demo, or learn what a pip is, are still checked, but they're where honest ads live.

Is it true for this geo and this account type?
Does it give the whole picture, including costs and risk?
Has the broker or network approved it in writing?

steps.h: Worked example: a true number that misleads
steps.p: Example: an ad says 'spreads from 0.0 pips'. That is true only on the raw account, which charges $7 commission per lot round trip. On EUR/USD one pip on a standard lot is about $10, so a typical 1.2 pip standard spread costs about $12. The 0.0 claim hides the $7.
steps.more: Pip values change with the pair and the account currency, so always use the broker's own cost table. The lesson is general: a number can be true and still mislead if it leaves out the cost that comes with it. Regulators in many places judge the overall impression, not each word on its own.

d.text: Example: '0.0 pips' sounds free, but the raw account costs $7 per lot in commission. The honest line: 'Raw spreads from 0.0 pips plus $7 commission per lot. Costs vary by account.'

steps.say: Here's a true number that misleads. An ad says spreads from zero point zero pips. That's true only on the raw account, which charges seven dollars commission per lot, round trip. On euro-dollar, one pip on a standard lot is about ten dollars, so a typical one point two pip standard spread costs about twelve dollars. The zero sounds free, but it hides the seven dollars. The honest line on screen reads: raw spreads from zero point zero pips plus seven dollars commission per lot, costs vary by account. Always use the broker's own cost table.

steps.h: Implied claims hide in the picture
steps.p: A claim does not need words. Reviewers and regulators look at the overall impression. These visuals tell the viewer 'this will make you rich' even when the text says nothing about money, so treat them as outcome claims.
d: Luxury props|cars, watches, villas, private jets
Cash|stacks of notes, bank app balances
Profit screenshots|green P&L, 'today's gains'
Only winning charts|arrows that only go up
Fake urgency|countdowns, 'last 3 spots'
Borrowed authority|news logos, celebrity faces
steps.say: A claim doesn't need words. Reviewers and regulators look at the overall impression. Look at the cards. Luxury props, like cars, watches, villas and private jets. Cash, like stacks of notes or bank app balances. Profit screenshots, a green P and L, profit and loss, or today's gains. Charts with arrows that only go up. Fake urgency, like countdowns or last three spots. And borrowed authority, like news logos and celebrity faces. These say this will make you rich, even when the text says nothing about money. Treat them as outcome claims.

steps.h: Why the words around the warning matter
steps.p: Module 2 showed where the risk warning goes. This lesson is about everything else you write. The copy decides who clicks. Clear, honest copy brings people who understand the product and the risk, and those are the people who pass KYC, deposit with open eyes and stay.

d.s: Write for the person who will still be a client in six months.

steps.h: The five parts of a trading ad
steps.p: Almost every good trading ad has these five parts, in this order. Each part has its own rules. Write them separately, then read the whole ad as a stranger would.
d: Hook|a real question or a useful fact
Body|one idea, plainly explained
Proof|a verifiable fact with a source
Risk line|the approved warning from Module 2
Call to action|a low-pressure next step
steps.say: Almost every good trading ad has five parts, in this order. Look at the cards. The hook: a real question or a useful fact. The body: one idea, plainly explained. The proof: a verifiable fact, with a source. The risk line: the approved warning from module two. And the call to action: a low-pressure next step. Each part has its own rules. Write them separately, then read the whole ad as a stranger would.

steps.h: Calls to action: pressure versus honest
steps.p: The call to action, or CTA, is the instruction at the end of the ad. Pressure CTAs promise outcomes or create panic. Honest CTAs describe exactly what happens when someone taps.

a.title: Pressure (avoid)
items: 'Start earning now'
'Claim your profits'
'Don't miss out, ends tonight'
'Join 10,000 winners'

b.title: Honest
items: 'Open a demo account'
'See the fees'
'Learn the basics'
'Read how it works'

steps.say: The call to action, or C T A, is the instruction at the end of the ad. On the left, pressure C T As to avoid: start earning now, claim your profits, don't miss out, ends tonight, join ten thousand winners. They promise outcomes or create panic. On the right, honest ones: open a demo account, see the fees, learn the basics, read how it works. Honest C T As describe exactly what happens when someone taps.

steps.say: Here are starting rules for numbers in trading copy, not legal advice. Costs: show spread and commission together. Minimum deposit: state it as a fact, only if true for the geo. Leverage: never as a benefit, and show the loss side. User counts are amber, and need a dated source. Returns or win rates are red, never. And bonus amounts only where legal, with key terms beside them. Every number needs a source from the broker for that geo, and some should never appear, however true they are for some users.

steps.h: Worked example: leverage cuts both ways
steps.p: Example: 'control $5,000 with just $50' sounds like a benefit. At 1:100 leverage, $50 controls a $5,000 position. A 1% move against you is $50, the whole deposit. Honest copy says that plainly or leaves leverage out.
steps.more: Leverage limits differ by country and account type; in the UK and EU, retail CFD leverage is capped at the time of writing, and many other regulators set limits too. Never present high leverage as a reason to sign up. If the broker's offer page leads with leverage, ask your manager whether you may leave it out of your ads.

d.text: Example: $50 × 100 = $5,000 position. 1% of $5,000 = $50. Honest line: 'With 1:100 leverage, a 1% move against you can wipe out a $50 deposit.'

The honest line reads: with one to one hundred leverage, a one percent move against you can wipe out a fifty dollar deposit. Leverage limits differ by country and account type. Never present high leverage as a reason to sign up. Say it plainly, or leave it out.

steps.h: Video: is the warning on screen long enough?
steps.p: Building on Module 2: the warning stays on screen for the whole clip. Check that the clip is long enough to read it. As a rough guide, assume about 3 words per second and give people time to read it twice.
steps.more: Example: a 7-word short warning needs about 7 ÷ 3 × 2 ≈ 5 seconds, so any clip over 5 seconds with the warning on screen throughout is fine. The full CFD warning is about 53 words: 53 ÷ 3 × 2 ≈ 35 seconds. That is why the full text usually goes on an end card and in the ad text as well. Rough guide only; it varies by viewer and language.

steps.h: Six honest angles for trading offers
steps.p: Each angle points to something the product really does or something the viewer really learns. None of them promise a result. Use only the ones that are true for your broker in your geo.

steps.h: The structure of an honest hook
steps.p: Most strong honest ads follow the same five beats. The hook earns attention with something real, the body delivers one useful idea, and the close points to a low-pressure next step like a demo or a lesson.

Give one useful fact
Show what the product does
State the risk plainly
Invite a low-pressure next step

steps.p: Honest angles can go wrong too, usually when the angle is a disguise. If the 'education' exists only to rush people into a deposit, reviewers and users notice, and the quality of your FTDs drops.

steps.h: Worked example: the angle test budget
steps.p: Example: your target cost per qualified FTD is $60. Each angle needs at least 2 × target to apply the zero-FTD kill, and 3 × target to judge CPA properly. Three angles at 3 × target is the full test.
steps.more: Example: 3 × $60 = $180 per angle. 3 angles × $180 = $540. Spread over 6 days that is $30 a day per ad set, or $90 a day in total. If $540 is more than you can afford to lose, test two angles, not three smaller ones. Trading FTDs often arrive days after the click, so leave a few days after the spend ends before final judgement.

Two angles pass: keep both, so fatigue on one does not stop you

steps.h: Your visuals speak before your words
steps.p: On a phone, people see the picture before they read a word. In trading ads the picture often decides whether the ad is approved and what kind of person clicks. A visual that implies wealth attracts the wrong users and invites rejection, however careful the text is.

d.b: Show the product, not the lifestyle
d.s: What people see is the first claim you make.

steps.say: Your visuals speak before your words. On a phone, people see the picture first. In trading ads, the picture often decides whether the ad is approved, and what kind of person clicks. A visual that implies wealth attracts the wrong users and invites rejection, however careful the text is. So show the product, not the lifestyle. What people see is the first claim you make.

steps.p: These visuals work as income or safety claims, and many are banned outright by platform policies for financial ads. Remove them from every creative, including thumbnails and the first frame of video.
d: Cash and luxury|notes, cars, watches, villas
Profit screens|green P&L, account balances
One-way charts|arrows that only go up
Fake media|news layouts, TV logos
Famous faces|celebrities, public figures
Before and after|'my balance then and now'
steps.say: These visuals work as income or safety claims, and many are banned outright by platform policies for financial ads. Look at the cards. Cash and luxury: notes, cars, watches, villas. Profit screens: a green P and L, profit and loss, or account balances. One-way charts, with arrows that only go up. Fake media, like news layouts and T V logos. Famous faces, celebrities and public figures. And before and after, my balance then and now. Remove them from every creative, including thumbnails and the first frame of video.

steps.p: Honest visuals show the product, explain an idea or show a real person speaking plainly. They are easy to approve and they set the right expectation for the person who clicks.

Cost card|one trade's cost shown in dollars
steps.say: Now the visuals that work honestly. A demo screen recording, with DEMO visible on screen. An explainer diagram, with leverage or spread drawn simply. Risk tools, like setting a stop-loss in the app. A real presenter talking to camera, with no props. Local context, like a person at a desk in Lagos or Nairobi. And a cost card, showing one trade's cost in dollars. They show the product, explain an idea, or show a real person speaking plainly. They're easy to approve, and they set the right expectation.

steps.p: In many places, testimonials about trading returns are restricted or banned in financial promotions, and influencers can be liable for what they say. When you use a real person, they talk about the experience of learning or using the tool, never about money made.

steps.p: UGC means user-generated content: a creator films a casual video in their own style for your ads. Module 2 covered influencer briefs; a UGC brief is shorter. Give it in writing before they film. Keep the chat; it is your proof of what you asked for if their draft goes wrong.

steps.h: Worked example: what 'zero fees' can hide
steps.p: Example: an exchange says 'zero fees' but builds a 1% spread into the price. A user buys $200 of bitcoin. They pay no labelled fee, but the price they get is about 1% worse, so the cost is about $2. Sell straight back and they lose about $4 in total.
steps.more: Spreads and fees vary by exchange, by coin and by payment method, and card or local transfer fees can add more. Always use the exchange's own fee page for the geo, and show a real cost example rather than the word 'free'.

d.text: Example: $200 buy × 1% spread ≈ $2. Buy and sell back ≈ $4. 'Zero fees' hides a real cost; say 'no trading fee; costs are included in the price'.

steps.h: Why you need a creative system
steps.p: Trading creatives fail in two ways: they get rejected, or they get approved and lose money. A simple, written system handles both. It catches risky claims before review and tells you exactly when to kill, keep, scale or refresh. Without it, decisions are made by mood.

d.b: One pipeline, one log, one rule card
d.s: Repeat it for every creative, even small edits.

steps.say: Why do you need a creative system? Trading creatives fail in two ways. They get rejected, or they get approved and lose money. A simple, written system handles both. It catches risky claims before review, and tells you exactly when to kill, keep, scale or refresh. Without it, decisions are made by mood. One pipeline, one log, one rule card, repeated for every creative, even small edits.

steps.p: Every creative follows the same path. Skipping a step to save time is how a rejected ad, a restricted account or a withheld payout happens. Each step leaves a line in your log.
d: Brief
Draft
Claim audit
Broker approval
Platform review
Test and log
steps.say: Every creative follows the same path. Follow the flow. Brief. Draft. Claim audit. Broker approval. Platform review. Then test and log. Each step leaves a line in your log. Skipping a step to save time is how a rejected ad, a restricted account or a withheld payout happens.

steps.p: A compliance log is a simple sheet with one row per creative. It is your evidence if a network, broker or platform asks questions months later. Store it where the whole team can see it.
steps.say: A compliance log is a simple sheet with one row per creative. Look at the example. Each row shows the ad, the warning version, who approved it and the date. Two Kenya ads were approved by the network's affiliate manager on the second of October. The Nigeria U G C ad is still pending, with no date. And the note: pending rows never go live. This log is your evidence if a network, broker or platform asks questions months later, so store it where the whole team can see it.

steps.p: Example: CTR of one creative over seven days while frequency rises. Fatigue is when the same people have seen it too often. A starting rule: refresh when CTR falls 30% below its first three-day average and frequency is above 2.5.

steps.p: Testing mistakes in trading cost more than in most verticals, because conversions arrive late and each one is expensive. These are the ones to watch.

Scaling an ad nobody has approved in writing

Judging on platform-reported results: decide on network-confirmed qualified F T Ds. Killing on day one because there are no F T Ds yet: no decisions before twenty four hours, no C P A kills before forty eight hours, and no scaling before seventy two. Re-uploading a rejected ad unchanged: fix the claim, then submit it as a new reviewed ad. Scaling an ad nobody approved in writing: every live ad has an approved row in the log.

steps.h: Your rule card for trading creatives
steps.p: Starting rules to adapt, using the Foundations rule card on network-confirmed qualified FTDs. Check from the top; the first rule that applies is the decision.
d: Kill: spend ≥ 2 × target with 0 qualified FTDs
Kill: after 3 × target spend, CPA > lower of 1.5 × target and break-even
Scale +30–50%: CPA ≤ 0.6 × target with ≥ 10 qualified FTDs
Scale +20% every ≥ 48h: CPA ≤ 0.8 × target with ≥ 3 qualified FTDs
Refresh: CTR 30% below first 3-day average and frequency > 2.5
Otherwise hold or keep. No decisions before 24h, no CPA kills before 48h, no scaling before 72h
steps.say: Here's your rule card for trading creatives, on network-confirmed qualified F T Ds. Check from the top, and the first rule that applies is the decision. Kill at two times target spend with zero F T Ds. Kill after three times target spend if C P A is above the lower of one point five times target and break-even. Scale thirty to fifty percent when C P A is point six times target or less, with ten or more F T Ds. Scale twenty percent, every forty eight hours or more, at point eight times target or less, with three or more. Refresh when C T R is thirty percent below its first three-day average and frequency is above two point five. Otherwise, hold or keep. And the timing rule from Foundations: no decisions before twenty four hours, no C P A kills before forty eight, and no scaling before seventy two. These are starting rules to adapt.

exam.q: Your 20-second video carries a 6-word short warning. Rough guide at 3 words per second read twice: is a lower third for the full video enough time?

options: No problem, it is a product fact
It sells leverage as a benefit; show the loss side or leave leverage out
exam.why: At 1:100, a 1% move against a $10,000 position is $100, the whole deposit. Leverage is never a selling point.

exam.why: $500 ÷ 10 = $50 and $500 ÷ 5 = $100. You are paid on qualified FTDs.
